item.title: Int'l biodiversity summit calls for stronger global action to protect nature
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18
YEREVAN, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- The UN chief and government officials called for accelerated global action to protect biodiversity at a summit held here on Friday, urging countries to turn international commitments into concrete measures and strengthen cooperation to address biodiversity loss. The Leaders' Summit on Biodiversity, themed "Leaders for Nature," brought together heads of state and government and representatives of international organizations ahead of the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17), scheduled for Oct. 19 to 30. Representatives of governments, non-governmental organizations, experts and other stakeholders also attended the summit. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres urged countries to show "more action, more speed, and more will" to protect biodiversity. "Halfway to 2030, Yerevan is our moment of accountability," Guterres said at the summit, calling for assessing progress toward global conservation targets laid out in the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework adopted in 2022. He warned that progress to halt biodiversity loss remained uneven and too slow, with financing and other support still falling short of what was needed. Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan highlighted the links between peace and biodiversity conservation. "Peace and biodiversity are of great significance, both domestically and across borders," Pashinyan said during a roundtable discussion held as part of the summit. He stressed that environmental challenges could not be addressed by any country alone, calling for greater international cooperation. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian also noted the importance of biodiversity conservation in the context of peace, security and sustainable development. He highlighted the environmental damage caused by armed conflicts and called for stronger international support for conservation efforts. Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev called for broad international cooperation to safeguard the world's natural heritage, stressing that "biodiversity sustains human well-being, economic resilience and long-term security." Chinese Minister of Ecology and Environment Huang Runqiu said China had consistently participated in global biodiversity governance with strong political commitment and concrete action, helping promote the adoption of the landmark Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. Huang called for greater financial, technological and capacity-building support for developing countries to ensure the framework's comprehensive, balanced and effective implementation. The summit adopted the Yerevan Declaration, entitled "Taking Action for Nature," which reaffirmed commitments to the Convention on Biological Diversity and to the effective implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, with its mission of halting and reversing biodiversity loss by 2030 and its vision of living in harmony with nature by 2050.■

item.title: Decades of restoration work breathes new life into once-vanished lake
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18
HOHHOT, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- In the core zone of a wetland in Ulanqab, north China's Inner Mongolia, a smart ecological supervision center deploys drone patrols and AI-powered wildlife tracking technology to help restore a lake that had once dried up. Autumn envelops the Huangqihai Lake with quiet vibrancy. Birds such as white-naped cranes wade across the muddy shallows in search of food. The lake spans 85.22 square km, according to the center's September figures. This vibrant landscape is almost unrecognizable from 2006, when the water dried up, and most of the lakebed was exposed. Even after water partially returned in 2012, the lake's size rarely exceeded 25 square km in the wettest months, and it shrank to less than 5 square km in dry seasons. The lake once ranked among eight major lakes in the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, forming a critical wetland in northern China. Back in the 1950s, it stretched across some 130 square km and sustained a thriving fishery. Its local specialty, Guancun crucian carp, once graced state banquets. But rising human activity and persistent drought reduced its size. "Huangqihai is coming back to life. Fish have returned, giving migratory birds a safe haven on their migrating journeys," said Wang Shaojun, with the administrative office of the Huangqihai Wetland Nature Reserve. He attributes the recovery to decades of targeted restoration efforts. The smart ecological supervision center launched in 2024 as the first of its kind in Inner Mongolia has transformed conservation work that once depended solely on human rangers. The system now generates over 100,000 monitoring data points each month, supplying scientific evidence to guide restoration decisions. Wildlife offers the most telling barometer of the lake's ecological recovery. In May 2025, schools of fish reappeared in the lake. The scene had not been seen for 27 years. Wang said this milestone signals the restoration of the lake's natural self-purification capacity and a functional aquatic food web. The center's AI-driven biodiversity system automatically identifies bird species from camera footage. This spring, the system captured images of a relict gull, a rare national Class-I protected species. The valuable footage provides conservation teams with important evidence to support field surveys and protection planning. So far, researchers have recorded 168 bird species within the reserve. Sensors linked to the smart system also track water levels, stream flow and pest density. Conservation staff use this data to run targeted pest control, keeping migratory birds safe. "The data-driven approach provides solid scientific grounding for targeted ecological management of the lake," Wang said. Inner Mongolia, home to four major deserts and four extensive sandy lands, is among the most severely desertified areas in China. The region has taken a leading role in the country's push to restore damaged ecosystems. Local farmer Lian Sixiong saw his irrigation practices shift in 2024. That year, local water authorities introduced irrigation water quotas for every village and household in the lake basin. Smart meters installed on irrigation wells track water use round the clock. "In the old days, all farmers here used flood irrigation to get the soil completely soaked," Lian recalled. "With new regulations on the water use, farmers are far more conscious about saving water," he said. Since 2021, local authorities have launched 44 restoration projects across the lake reserve, including riverway dredging, wildlife habitat rehabilitation, agricultural pollution mitigation, waste treatment and sewage-treatment infrastructure upgrades. As a result, the lake receives no industrial or domestic wastewater. Residential waste and sewage are fully treated on a daily basis. "Though the lake has not recovered to its 1950s scale, above-normal precipitation in recent years has improved regional water recharge conditions. Coupled with effective conservation efforts, this will accelerate the lake's recovery," Wang said. ■

item.title: Feature: As tigers return, technology protects wildlife and people who share their habitat
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18
CHANGCHUN/HARBIN, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- A tigress moved through the forest, followed by five cubs, their small bodies weaving through the undergrowth. This rare scene was captured by an infrared camera in the Northeast China Tiger and Leopard National Park (NCTLNP) late last year. It was the first recorded footage in China of a wild Siberian tiger accompanied by an unusually large litter of five cubs, offering a glimpse into the recovery of these endangered big cats. Transmitted to the park's monitoring center in real time, the footage became part of a growing body of data that helps conservation workers identify individual animals and track their movements without having to follow them deep into the forest. Latest monitoring shows that three of the tigress's five cubs have already left their mother's side, while the other two are still with her. Siberian tigers, also known as Amur tigers, along with Amur leopards, are flagship species for biodiversity conservation and important indicators of a healthy ecosystem. Following a pilot phase launched in 2017, the NCTLNP was officially established in 2021 as one of the first five national parks in China. Leveraging new technology, this park has built an integrated monitoring system that combines satellite remote sensing, ground-based infrared cameras and aerial surveillance involving drones, covering most of its 14,100-square-kilometer area across Jilin and Heilongjiang provinces in China's northeast. A major challenge in building such a system is network coverage. The park has established 95 wireless communication base stations and deployed around 30,000 cameras, according to Sun Pengyu, the person responsible for the forestry and grassland sector at Jishi Media, the main constructor of the system. Wireless data transmission covers more than 80 percent of the park area, allowing footage to reach the park administration within roughly a minute of being captured, Sun said. Empowered by artificial intelligence, the system can identify more than 30 wildlife species and make preliminary identifications of individual tigers and leopards based on their distinctive coat patterns, said Chen Xiaocai, head of the park administration's comprehensive office. Researchers then cross-check the initial identifications against other biological features, including facial contours, to verify each animal's identity and build individual profiles for further research and conservation work, Chen added. The park has also restored forest habitats and improved ecological connectivity. Along the China-Russia border, more than 290 sections of fencing in areas frequented by tigers and leopards have been removed, helping reopen cross-border routes for wildlife. The latest monitoring data show that the number of wild Siberian tigers in the park has risen from 27 in 2017 to 72, while the wild Amur leopard population has grown from 42 to 115. Sightings of other wildlife, including deer and roe deer, offer further indications of an ecosystem supporting the return of its top predators. For Li Gang, deputy head of Chaoyanggou forest farm in Dongning, Heilongjiang Province, the changes brought by technology are tangible. Li has worked at the forest farm, also a core conservation area, since 2009. In the early years, maintaining infrared cameras meant trekking into the mountains to replace batteries and retrieve memory cards. This process not only delayed access to information but also exposed staff to risks posed by rugged terrain and encounters with large predators. "On one occasion, I walked 17 kilometers carrying about 200 batteries and spare cameras," he recalled. Now, cameras equipped with wireless transmission can send images and video directly to a central platform. Satellite imagery helps workers assess habitat conditions across large areas, while drones can inspect remote terrain, check for suspected forest fires and investigate possible illegal activities. Li has also seen changes in the wildlife around him. "Sika deer were scarce in the area when I began working here, but during a recent outing, I saw more than 100," Li said. As tigers and leopards reclaim more territory, protecting them also means keeping people safe. In parts of the national park, villages and wildlife habitats overlap, making early warnings an important part of conservation. Cameras near settlements can detect tigers, leopards, bears and wild boars entering designated risk areas. Alerts are then sent to patrol teams and nearby residents, giving people time to avoid potentially dangerous encounters. In Dongning, information can also be shared via local chat groups, allowing rangers to warn residents when a tiger is spotted. For Li and his colleagues, such technology does not replace fieldwork for rangers, but it helps make patrols more targeted, reducing unnecessary journeys into sensitive habitats. "We want to give people and wildlife room to live without disturbing one another, for the benefit of both," Li said. ■

item.title: Chinese embassy condemns Japanese leaders' Yasukuni Shrine moves as affront to historical justice: spokesperson
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18
TOKYO, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- A spokesperson for the Chinese Embassy in Japan on Saturday strongly condemned Japan's latest negative moves concerning the war-linked Yasukuni Shrine, after Japanese leaders sent ritual offerings to the shrine and some cabinet members and lawmakers visited it. Japan launched wars of aggression against other countries and regions during World War II and committed heinous crimes, the spokesperson said in response to media inquiries. The so-called Yasukuni Shrine enshrines 14 Class-A war criminals directly responsible for the wars of aggression and is a spiritual tool and symbol of Japanese militarism, the spokesperson said. No matter what excuses Japanese officials make for paying homage to the shrine, they cannot conceal their true intentions of rehabilitating war criminals, covering up wartime crimes, distorting historical facts and paving the way for accelerating Japan's remilitarization, the spokesperson said. Such erroneous acts desecrate historical justice, challenge the bottom line of human civilization and constitute a provocation to the postwar international order, drawing firm opposition from the international community, the spokesperson added. Noting that this year marks the 80th anniversary of the opening of the Tokyo Trials, the spokesperson said that a correct understanding of and attitude toward history are essential for Japan's return to the international community after the war, constitute a political foundation for its relations with neighboring countries, and serve as a yardstick for assessing whether Japan honors its commitment to peaceful development. China solemnly urges Japan to deeply reflect on its history of aggression, face up to its wartime crimes, exercise prudence in words and deeds on issues concerning the Yasukuni Shrine, and completely break with militarism, the spokesperson said, calling on the Japanese side to win the trust of its Asian neighbors and the international community through concrete actions. ■

item.title: Liangzhu forum opens, highlights heritage conservation, int'l cooperation
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18
HANGZHOU, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- The fourth Liangzhu Forum opened Sunday in Hangzhou, east China's Zhejiang Province, to discuss challenges in cultural heritage conservation and paths to deepen international cooperation. The year 2026 marks the 90th anniversary of the discovery of the Liangzhu ruins. Themed "Bridging the Past and the Future: Safeguarding Cultural Heritage for Our Times," the forum brings together officials, archaeologists and scholars from around the world. Experts and scholars will discuss topics ranging from early civilizations to archaeological research on ancient cities, with new research findings and advances also set to be unveiled, Zhang Ling, an official with China's National Cultural Heritage Administration, said at an earlier briefing. Participants will address challenges including the loss of cultural heritage, advances in technologies for protecting and utilizing cultural relics, and sustainable tourism, Zhang added. Lina Mendoni, Minister of Culture of Greece, said in a speech at the opening ceremony that people must move beyond traditional approaches and adopt adaptive, preventive and holistic management to safeguard cultural heritage. "UNESCO believes that sustainable tourism can help safeguard cultural heritage by raising awareness of the importance of heritage for future generations, improving cultural understanding and strengthening local livelihoods," said Nayef Al-Fayez, UNESCO Assistant Director-General for Culture, in his video speech. The forum brings together four international organizations: UNESCO, based in Paris; the International Centre for the Study of the Preservation and Restoration of Cultural Property, headquartered in Rome; the Alliance for Cultural Heritage in Asia, based in Beijing; and the International Alliance for the Protection of Heritage, headquartered in Geneva. The gathering marks a step for the forum to turn into a broader venue for multilateral dialogue on cultural heritage, said Wen Dayan, another official with the National Cultural Heritage Administration. This year's event includes an opening ceremony and main forum, five sub-forums and five companion events, including an international artists' creative tour exhibition, a Liangzhu cultural and creative market, a design exhibition and international dialogues. Inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2019, the Archaeological Ruins of Liangzhu City offer important evidence of an early regional state that flourished more than 5,000 years ago. The inaugural forum was held in Hangzhou in 2023. The fourth edition runs through Tuesday and is co-hosted by China's Ministry of Culture and Tourism, the National Cultural Heritage Administration and the Zhejiang provincial government. ■

item.title: China railway passenger trips hit record high in first three quarters
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-18
BEIJING, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- China's railway network handled 3.71 billion passenger trips in the first three quarters of 2026, up 4.8 percent year on year, the highest for the period, according to the China State Railway Group Co., Ltd. (China Railway). During the period, the railway network operated an average of 11,511 passenger trains daily, up 5.3 percent from a year earlier. Railway departments have actively responded to demand for sightseeing, wellness tours and red-themed study tours, according to China Railway. In the first nine months, a total of 2,860 tourist trains were operated across the country, up 25.5 percent year on year. The railway network also operated 947 special trains for concertgoers and sports fans during the period, effectively boosting the catering, hotel and cultural tourism sectors. Cross-border rail travel also continued to grow. The China-Laos Railway carried 265,000 cross-border trips, up 37.8 percent, while the Guangzhou-Shenzhen-Hong Kong high-speed railway handled over 25.8 million cross-border trips, up 11.8 percent, China Railway said. China Railway also adapted to the inbound travel boom created by the country's visa-free transit policy. The railway network carried over 19 million foreign passenger trips in the first three quarters, up 33.4 percent year on year, the company said. Behind the steady growth in passenger traffic is China's increasingly dense high-speed rail network. By the end of 2025, the country's total operating railway mileage had reached 165,000 km, which included more than 50,000 km of high-speed rail. On Sept. 28, China opened four high-speed rail sections, connecting Xiongan in north China's Hebei Province with Shangqiu in Henan Province in central China, Xi'an with Ankang in Shaanxi Province in northwest China, Yichang with Xingshan in central China's Hubei Province, and Harbin with Yichun in Heilongjiang Province in the country's northeast. China's high-speed rail network is projected to hit 70,000 km by 2035, featuring eight north-south vertical lines and eight east-west horizontal lines. Once complete, the network will connect major cities, city clusters and key economic zones across the country. ■

item.title: Xinhua Headlines: "China Magnet" attracts growing interest from global talent
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-17
* A growing number of foreign professionals are drawn to China by its expanding career opportunities, as the country's fast-growing industries strengthen its appeal amid economic pressures in some overseas markets. Positive experiences shared by foreign visitors on social media are also helping improve global perceptions of China. * China's emerging industries, from artificial intelligence and robotics to new energy, are strengthening the pull of innovation, offering international professionals opportunities to put their expertise into practice. * As Chinese technology companies expand globally, their growing demand for international expertise is creating career opportunities beyond China's borders. BEIJING, Oct. 17 (Xinhua) -- For 33-year-old Federico Flamenco, a Salvadoran engineer working in China's robotics industry, a once-distant career dream has become a reality. "Working in robotics is something I could once only dream about. Now I work with robotic arms and get to see how quickly humanoid robots are developing here in China," he said. After earning a bachelor's degree in El Salvador, Flamenco pursued a master's degree in electrical engineering in China. Currently at JAKA Robotics, a Chinese robotics company, he helps overseas customers find suitable robotic solutions, drawing on his engineering expertise and knowledge of Spanish, English, Chinese and Portuguese. Flamenco is among a growing number of foreign professionals drawn to China by expanding career opportunities, as its fast-growing industries strengthen the country's appeal amid economic pressures in some overseas markets. Positive experiences shared by foreign visitors on social media are also helping improve perceptions of China abroad. CHINA ON THE RADAR Miriam Wickertsheim, general manager of Direct HR, a recruitment firm that helps international companies in China hire senior executives, has seen the shift firsthand. "Global interest in working in China has more than doubled this year compared with two years ago, with a major surge in inquiries in early summer," said Wickertsheim. "We receive numerous inquiries from jobseekers in Europe, Australia, Arab countries, the United States and South America," she said, attributing the growing interest to a combination of "push and pull" factors. In developed economies, sluggish growth and rising inflation have prompted more professionals to seek opportunities abroad, Wickertsheim explained. Layoffs at major technology companies have also driven skilled workers to explore other job markets, she added. Meanwhile, professionals from countries such as those in South America admire China's rapid development and robust business ecosystem and hope to achieve joint growth with China, said Wickertsheim. Wickertsheim noted that emerging industries such as biotechnology, pharmaceuticals and industrial automation are becoming increasingly important to her firm's recruitment business, while intelligent factories and robotic automation are emerging as key business areas. Beyond career prospects, social media is also reshaping perceptions of China, Wickertsheim said. While Western media coverage of China has often focused on controversies, the country's 30-day visa-free entry policy has enhanced its appeal to foreign visitors, who share real, positive personal experiences online, she said. "People saw China's safe, clean, modern environment, friendly locals and delicious food," she said, adding that these positive impressions have become another key factor drawing international talent to the country. PULL OF INNOVATION China's fast-growing emerging industries, from artificial intelligence and robotics to new energy, are strengthening the pull of innovation, offering international professionals opportunities to put their expertise into practice. Cao Jun, chief financial officer of Hydrexia, a Chinese hydrogen energy company, said a major strength of Chinese technology enterprises lies in their ability to closely integrate technological innovation, product manufacturing and practical applications. In the hydrogen energy sector, China's relatively complete industrial chain and strong engineering and manufacturing capabilities allow international professionals to participate in every stage, from research and development to manufacturing and commercialization in overseas markets, Cao said. China's push for innovation-driven growth extends across its economy. In the first half of 2026, the country's GDP grew 4.7 percent year-on-year, with new growth drivers, including high-end manufacturing, the digital economy and modern services, contributing more than 40 percent to economic growth, official data showed. China last week issued guidelines aimed at accelerating the development of new quality productive forces, calling for measures like closer integration of technological and industrial innovation and improved talent development mechanisms. Such industrial policies also offer clues to where China's economy is headed. "The best industry development reference for foreign businesses and jobseekers comes from China's five-year development plans, which outline the country's investment priorities and emerging track directions," Wickertsheim said. "More global enterprise executives and board members are now proactively learning about China's industrial policies, unlike in the past," she said. "This improved understanding helps foreign companies formulate more scientific China market strategies." OPPORTUNITIES BEYOND BORDERS As Chinese technology companies expand globally, their growing demand for international expertise is creating career opportunities beyond China's borders. Hydrexia has expanded into overseas markets including the United States, Australia and Southeast Asia, building international teams that bring together employees familiar with Chinese technology and manufacturing as well as those with expertise in local markets. Cao said the company aims to develop overseas teams that can serve local customers over the long term and become part of local hydrogen energy industries, rather than merely act as sales outlets for Chinese products. Hydrexia employs about 250 people worldwide, with overseas business teams accounting for around 10 percent of its workforce. It plans to strengthen overseas teams over the next two to three years. By the end of 2025, Chinese investors had established more than 50,000 overseas enterprises across 190 countries and regions, with China's cumulative outbound investment ranking among the world's top three for nine consecutive years. Chinese companies operating abroad have created an average of over 2 million jobs annually, according to the Ministry of Commerce. China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) calls for improving support services for enterprises operating overseas and encouraging eligible companies to carry out mutually beneficial overseas investment cooperation. Wickertsheim said Direct HR has received increased inquiries from Chinese companies planning to expand overseas. She expects Chinese multinational enterprises to generate substantial demand for overseas recruitment over the next five years. ■

item.title: Xi stresses prioritizing ecological conservation, pursuing green development
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16
Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, visits the Huangqihai Lake nature reserve in Ulanqab, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, Oct. 16, 2026. Xi made an inspection trip on Friday to the city of Ulanqab, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. (Xinhua/Yan Yan) ULANQAB, Inner Mongolia, Oct. 16 (Xinhua) -- Chinese President Xi Jinping has emphasized the need to unswervingly follow the path of prioritizing ecological conservation and pursuing green development. Xi, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks during an inspection trip on Friday to the city of Ulanqab, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. Huangqihai Lake in Ulanqab was once on the verge of drying up due to climate and other impacts. After years of comprehensive conservation, its water body has gradually been restored and expanded. During the inspection trip, Xi visited the Huangqihai Lake nature reserve, where he was briefed on Inner Mongolia's efforts to strengthen ecological conservation, and inspected the lake's shoreline and mudflats and observed birds inhabiting the area. He stressed the need to fully implement the country's wetland protection law, firmly uphold ecological red lines, and safeguard biodiversity. For degraded wetland ecosystems, he called for giving priority to natural restoration, supplemented by human intervention, and carrying out restoration in a scientific and sound manner. Xi visited Chahar High Tech Development Zone in Ulanqab, and learned about Inner Mongolia's progress in advancing the construction of a hub for the "East Data, West Computing" project and the development of the green computing power industry. Noting that implementing the "East Data, West Computing" project and building a national integrated computing power network is an important decision made by the CPC Central Committee, Xi stressed the need to ensure the efficient operation of completed projects and finish the construction of follow-up projects on schedule. He called on all parties to earnestly implement the requirements for efficient, green and safe development, actively promote the development of the green computing power industry, and make greater contributions to building Digital China and developing new quality productive forces. Xi also viewed displays of local agricultural and livestock specialties, encouraging local authorities to better align production with sales to help farmers and herders increase their incomes. ■ Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, talks with staff members while visiting Chahar High Tech Development Zone in Ulanqab, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, Oct. 16, 2026.
